newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish inflation falls but rate cut still on hold.
newsitem.headline: Polish inflation falls but rate cut still on hold.

text.p: Polish inflation fell more than one point in April to year-on-year 15.3 percent but analysts said an official interest rate cut should not be expected because credit action continued to expand.

The Central Statistical Office (GUS) said earlier on Thursday prices grew one percent in April and 5.9 percent since start 1997, against a 8.9 percent rise in the CPI index duing the same period of last year.

"A first half interest rate change is not likely despite the fall in inflation as the central bank is concerned about growing consumer demand," said Stephen Pettyfer, Polish analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

The National Bank of Poland has twice increased obligatory reserves in 1997 to keep credit rates from falling in line with inflation but credit action continued to be the fastest growing component of money supply.
In the January-April period broad money supply as a whole grew 6.7 percent against a 11.6 percent rise in credit action.
Analysts said Poland's credit expansion was difficult to slow because disposable incomes had grown in recent years and Poles want more consumer goods.

"Personal credit continues to rise rapidly and corporate loans are growing quicker than in the same period of 1996, putting a break on any cuts in interest rates," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Bank in Warsaw.
Poland's official rates, at 25 percent for the Lombard and 22 percent for the discount rate, have not been reduced since July 1996, when year-on-year inflation stood at 20.4 percent.
Analysts reiterated a third quarter interest rate cut could be possible if inflation continued to fall to about year-on-year 14.5 percent in June.

April's inflation data also bode well for meeting the government's 13 percent price growth target in 1997, which the central said was achievable this year after previous targets were repeatedly overshot.

They said the rapid fall of the CPI index from 18.5 percent last December was caused by increased foreign competition after importer-taxes were reduced, slowly rising food prices and lower inflationary expectations among Poles.

"Prices of services, which are non-tradable and closely linked to increases of controlled prices, are keeping the CPI index from falling further amid low food price growth and cheap import inflows," ING's Rybinski said.
In the January-April period service prices have grown 11.1 percent and were at year-on-year 19.6 percent in April.
